## Why CW Framework Breaks Down

Now let's answer the why behind this problem. Mathematically, linear covariance propagation truncates 
the Taylor series expansion of the two-body equations of motion at first order, ignoring higher-order nonlinear 
terms. This truncation makes how we choose our coordinates critical to how well a linear model will track the true 
dynamics. In the CW framework, the dynamics are linearized around a circular chief orbit, assuming small 
offsets in a rotating RIC frame. These assumptions are valid for short time horizons, but as the time horizon evolves and 
separation increases, the truncated nonlinear terms become more present in the true system dynamics. As a result, the sample cloud 
bends into a "banana" shape. This is why we see the nonlinear Radial state in @fig-ric_time, as the In-Track separation increases, the Deputy's 
true path curves downward in the Radial direction. @fig-ric_2 shows the distribution of the propagated states in a formation with 10 m separation. 
We can see that the nonlinear terms don't have a noticeable effect until later in the simulation, which is what we would expect.

![Radial/In-Track Dispersion Over 30 Orbits.](images/ric_frame_propagation_animation2.gif){#fig-ric_2 width="80%" fig-align="center"}

Relative Orbital Elements do a better job at handling linear propagation because their state representation aligns more closely with the geometry of an orbit compared to the rotating RIC frame. Earlier, we discussed 
how the elements of $\mathbf{\Phi}_{ROE}$ are either static or drifting In-Track at a constant rate. The drift term $\mathbf{\Phi}_{ROE[1,0]} = -\frac{3}{2}nt$ can be understood 
by thinking about how an object orbits Earth. A simple thought experiment to understand objects in orbit is to imagine standing at the top of the mountain throwing a ball in a world with no air resistance. 
No matter how hard you throw the ball horizontally, the ball will be pulled downward due to gravity creating a parabolic trajectory. Now imagine being able to throw the ball so fast that the planet's curvature 
downwards matches the rate at which the ball is falling. For every meter the ball drops, the planet also curves away beneath it by the same amount. When these rates match perfectly, the ball 
will be in an orbit around the planet. 

![Orbits Thought Experiment. *Diagram generated with Gemini.*](images/orbit.jpg){#fig-orbit width="80%" fig-align="center"}

The speed needed to remain in orbit around the planet decreases the further away you get. If two objects are in orbit, the second being higher than the first, 
the second object will be moving slower than the first. If you are looking at the second object from the first, it will appear that the second object is drifting backwards. This is what $-\frac{3}{2}nt$ 
is showing: a positive $a_c \delta a$ will result in a negative drift rate.

The constant terms in $\mathbf{\Phi}_{ROE}$ are expected in a two-body simulation where there are no perturbing forces except gravity. We can see that the ROE framework does a 
really good job at representing what we would expect in a two-body simulation. As a result, the linear covariance propagation using $\mathbf{\Phi}_{ROE}$ is able to track the samples from the 
Monte Carlo simulation.
